newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: British family seek news of abducted son in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: British family seek news of abducted son in Cambodia.

text.p: A British family on Monday issued a fresh appeal for news of their abducted son, two months after their hopes had been briefly raised by reports that he had escaped from Khmer Rouge guerrillas in northern Cambodia.

Roy and Betty Howes, in a letter published by the Cambodia Daily, asked anyone with information about their 37-year-old son, Christopher, to contact the British Embassy in Phnom Penh or his employers, the British Mines Advisory Group (MAG).

"It is now 300 days since our son Christopher was abducted while working, at great personal risk, on mine clearance in Cambodia," Roy and Betty Howes wrote of the March 26 seizure of the mine clearance supervisor and his interpreter, Houn Hourth.

The two were part of a team working at a village north of the ancient Angkor temples in the northwest province of Siem Reap, and officials in the province believe they were later taken to the Khmer Rouge guerrilla base of Anlong Veng.

"After such a long period without firm news of his fate or whereabouts, Christopher's family and his friends wait anxiously for some hard evidence to become available," said the appeal. It made no mention of reports in November that Howes had escaped.
Their appeal follows a British government request to Thailand earlier this month to help gather information about Howes.
On November 21, deputy chief of staff Lieutenant-General Nhiek Bun Chhay said Howes and his interpreter had escaped from Anlong Veng with the help of Khmer Rouge defectors.
Nhiek Bun Chhay said he had been told through a Khmer Rouge go-between that the men were healthy but thin, and he thought they would arrive in Phnom Penh soon.
But the men failed to show up and three attempts to meet the hostages at different locations were unsuccessful.
Major General Khan Savoeun, head of search operations for Howes, told Reuters on Monday he believed Howes was in Khmer Rouge hands. He did not elaborate.
Khieu Samphan, nominal leader of the Khmer Rouge hardliners, has denied that his guerrillas were involved in the kidnapping.
The Khmer Rouge, who ruled Cambodia by terror from 1975-79, fought the coalition government that emerged after U.N.-run general elections in 1993.
The guerrilla movement has been badly hit by mass defections and only some 2,000 rebels are believed to be left in the north.
